full_judgment:
"A limitation law fixes upon a reasonable time within which a party is allowed to bring suit to recover his rights, and, if he fails to do so, establishes a legal presumption against him that he has no rights in the premises. It is a statute of repose. Every government is bound in good faith to furnish its citizens all needful legal remedies; but it is not bound to keep its courts open indefinitely for one who neglects or refuses to apply for redress until it may fairly be presumed that the means by which the other party might disprove the claim are lost in the lapse of time." 

 48. It has also been argued on behalf of the respondent bank that the consequence of the failure to file a suit within the prescribed period has been provided by section 46(5) such as to taking disciplinary action against the concerned officer of the financial institution and not that the plaint is to be rejected. But if the filing of the suit within the prescribed period is not mandatory and for that matter the suit being filed out of time is not affected at all, it will be practically unnecessary, futile and unreasonable to take any disciplinary action against the concerned officer of the financial institution. In that case, virtually there will be no limitation of time in filing any suit under the Ain. Consequently, the other provisions of section 46 will be of no use and shall be rendered unnecessary and redundant. It has already been observed that no law, particularly dealing with the civil rights can be conceived without the provisions of limitation. But the reasonable Legislature cannot enact such an unreasonable legislation having no rational nexus between its provisions and the objective intended to be achieved, while, like other legislations, the Ain also enjoys the presumption of constitutional validity. Therefore, the provision of section 46 (5) does not diminish the force of the other provisions of section 46 of the Ain. Accordingly, the filing of the suit within the period of limitation prescribed under sections 46(1) or section 46(3), as the case may be, is mandatory, which also contemplates implied nullification for disobeying the same provisions.
